query: What baseline hazard, censoring distribution, and site ICC should we assume to compute time‑to‑event sample size for breakthrough UTI in pediatric VUR?

response.query: What baseline hazard, censoring distribution, and site ICC should we assume to compute time‑to‑event sample size for breakthrough UTI in pediatric VUR?
response.answer: Assume an exponential baseline hazard, uniform censoring distribution, and site ICC of 0.05 for pediatric VUR breakthrough UTI sample size computation.

results.title: Design and analysis of cluster randomized trials with time-to-event outcomes under the additive hazards mixed model
results.content: First, we discuss improved inference for the treatment effect parameter via bias-corrected sandwich variance estimators and randomization-based test under AHMM, addressing potential small-sample biases in CRTs. Next, we derive a new sample size formula for AHMM analysis of CRTs accommodating both equal and unequal cluster sizes. Their sample size formula relies on the ICC defined based on the censoring indicators instead of the failure times, which may not fully capture the dependency structure of the time-to-event outcomes.13 To date, the optimal definition of the ICC for censored survival outcomes is debatable.14 Zhong and Cook13 refined the sample size formula under the marginal Cox proportional hazards model by numerically computing the asymptotic sandwich variance expression of the hazard ratio estimator, based on the assumed bivariate survival functions for the failure times as well as for the censoring times induced by copulas, but under equal cluster sizes. With non-censored continuous or binary outcomes, the sandwich variance estimator of the traditional GEE estimator has been shown to have negative bias and inflate the type I error rate of the Wald _z_- or _t_-test when the number of clusters is small.28 To maintain the nominal level of rejection under the null (and to ensure validity of the test), appropriate analysis of CRTs should account for such finite-sample bias in variance estimation, possibly through a bias-corrected sandwich variance estimator.28–31 Although there are several previous studies reporting simulation comparisons of different bias-corrected sandwich variance estimators for CRT applications,24,26,42,43 their development and findings are currently restricted to non-censored outcomes. Empirical type I error rates for the Wald _t_-test and randomization test from a simulation study based on different parameter configurations of the baseline hazard (_λ_ 0(_t_)), frailty variance (_σ_ 2), average cluster size , and estimated number of clusters when the coefficient of variation of cluster size is 0. Predicted and empirical power for the Wald _t_-test and randomization test from a simulation study based on different parameter configurations of the baseline hazard (_λ_ 0(_t_)), effect size (_δ_), frailty variance (_σ_ 2), average cluster size , and estimated number of clusters when the coefficient of variation of cluster size is 0. Second, while the statistical analysis with all bias-corrected sandwich variance estimators and the randomization test can easily accommodate cluster-level or participant-level covariates, our sample size procedure assumes an unadjusted AHMM without additional covariates.

results.title: Minimum sample size calculations for external validation of a clinical prediction model with a time‐to‐event outcome - Riley - 2022 - Statistics in Medicine - Wiley Online Library
results.content: A simulation-based framework is proposed, which calculates the sample size required to target a particular confidence interval width for the calibration slope measuring the agreement between predicted risks (from the model) and observed risks (derived using pseudo-observations to account for censoring) on the log cumulative hazard scale. We recently published two articles in *Statistics in Medicine* that describe how to calculate the minimum sample size for external validation of a clinical prediction model with either a continuous outcome,4 or with a binary outcome.5 The sample size criteria is based on ensuring precise estimation of key measures of a model's predictive performance in external validation, including calibration and—for binary outcomes—discrimination and net benefit. In Section 3 we propose a simulation-based framework for identifying the sample size that targets a precise estimate of calibration (in terms of calibration slope and calibration curves) at a particular time point, which requires the user to specify the anticipated overall event risk at that time, the distribution of the prediction model's linear predictor and the censoring and event distribution. We now consider how to calculate the sample size for a cohort study aiming to precisely estimate the calibration slope, assuming that the validation dataset will contain observations censored before the time point of interest for prediction. For example, we suggest using trial and error (or a simple one parameter non-linear optimization strategy) to identify the value of that gives the desired at the time point of interest in a large simulated dataset of survival times from an assumed exponential distribution with baseline rate parameter and a single covariate for whose corresponding parameter value is 1 (ie, assuming risks from the existing prediction model will have a perfect calibration slope across all time points). Pavlou et al suggest that sample size for validation of time-to-event prediction models can follow the sample size required for logistic prediction models “when the proportion of censored observations is high”.10 To examine this in the VTE example, we applied the closed-form sample size approach of Riley et al for validation of a logistic regression prediction model (with 3-year predicted risks generated from VTE model),5 and this calculates that 1203 individuals (about 203 events) are required for a target SE of 0.102 for the calibration slope.

results.title: Sample size calculation for studies with grouped survival data - PMC
results.content: Motivated by studies in HIV trials, cancer trials and in vitro experiments to study drug toxicity, we develop a sample size formula for studies with grouped survival endpoints that use the method of Prentice and Gloeckler for comparing two arms under the proportional hazards assumption. The sample size formula only requires estimates of the hazard ratio and survival probabilities of the event time of interest and the censoring time at the endpoints of the grouping intervals for one of the two arms. Inoue and Parmigiani8 and Raab et al9 discussed the design of such trials but focused on the design of follow-up intervals based on parametric models for the survival time instead of sample size determination for group comparisons. We derive a sample size formula for clinical trials with grouped survival data, based on the Wald test for the logarithm of the hazard ratio in a proportional hazards model and the method of Prentice and Gloeckler for data analysis. Finally, compared with the sample size calculation in trials with right censored data, we only need estimates of the baseline survival distribution at the finite number of visit times instead of the whole survival curve, which is due to the grouped nature of the data. By the aforementioned formula, we can determine the sample size if we have estimates of the effect size *β*, the distribution function of the survival time in the control group (*Z* = 0) and the distribution of the censoring time, both at the endpoints of the intervals. If we assume 15% lost to follow-up before the last visit time (36 month), which is the case in the trial in the work of Flynn et al,11 and if we assume the 15% lost to follow-up is uniformly distributed in 0, 36), then the sample sizes needed are 232 and 310, for a power of 0.8 and 0.9, with equal randomization, and these numbers become 218 and 291, if the randomization probability is 2∕3 for the vaccine group. To calculate the sample size, only estimates of the hazard ratio and the distributions of the survival time and censoring time at the endpoints of the grouping intervals are needed.
